questions.q: What is the core difference between imperative automation (Chapters 1-4) and declarative Infrastructure as Code?
options: Imperative specifies the steps to take; declarative specifies the desired end state and lets the tool compute the steps
Imperative and declarative are two names for the exact same approach
Declarative automation cannot provision real cloud resources
Imperative automation can only run on Windows, never on Linux or macOS
questions.explain: Imperative code (PowerShell, Python, CLI scripts) says what to do, in order. Declarative IaC says what should exist, and the tool figures out how to get there.

questions.q: Why does running New-AzStorageAccount a second time risk an error or a duplicate, while re-running an equivalent Bicep declaration does not?
options: The PowerShell command is a one-time instruction with no built-in idempotency; the declarative tool compares desired state to actual state and does nothing once they already match
Bicep cannot actually create storage accounts, only describe them
PowerShell cmdlets are always idempotent by default
There is no real difference in behavior between the two
questions.explain: Idempotency is a core, built-in feature of declarative IaC tools. An imperative cmdlet has no memory of prior runs unless you code that check yourself.

options: When a live resource's actual state no longer matches what was declared or last deployed
A type of network latency issue in Azure
An error that occurs only when using Python scripts
A deprecated feature of the Azure Portal
questions.explain: Drift happens when something changes a resource outside of your automation — a manual Portal edit, for example — so reality no longer matches the declared configuration.

questions.q: Which of these is a real, built-in drift-detection command mentioned in this lesson?
options: az deployment group what-if
New-AzStorageAccount -WhatIf -Drift
python detect_drift.py
az cli --check-reality
questions.explain: az deployment group what-if compares live Azure resources against a declared template and reports differences without applying anything. Terraform's terraform plan and AWS's aws cloudformation detect-stack-drift do the same job for their platforms.

questions.q: According to this lesson, are the imperative scripts taught in Chapters 1-4 now obsolete?
options: No — plenty of real automation, like scheduled tasks and compliance checks, is correctly imperative, and Chapter 6 returns to exactly that
Yes — declarative IaC replaces every use case for scripts
Yes, because scripts cannot run on cloud infrastructure
No, but only because PowerShell is required for all Azure work
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames declarative IaC as solving a different problem (drift, end-state management) — not as a replacement for every imperative use case.
